t: Minimum Number of Operations to Reinitialize a Permutation: Cycle Hunting
o: Starting from the identity permutation perm[i] = i on an even n, each operation rebuilds the array as arr[i] = perm[i/2] for even i and arr[i] = perm[n/2 + (i-1)/2] for odd i, and we must return the smallest positive number of applications that restores identity. Example n = 4: one operation yields [0,2,1,3] and a second restores [0,1,2,3], so the answer is 2; n = 2 needs 1 and n = 6 needs 4. Since n <= 1000, simulating whole arrays until they match is perfectly viable; but the operation is a fixed bijection whose cycle structure can be exploited — positions 0 and n - 1 never move, and every middle index marches along a cycle, so tracking a single well-chosen index until it first returns gives exactly the required count.
k: The operation is a permutation applied repeatedly, so identity returns after L steps where L is the lcm of all cycle lengths.
Positions 0 and n - 1 are fixed points; middle indices move under a map conjugate to multiplying by 2 modulo n - 1.
Every cycle length divides the cycle length of index 1 (the multiplicative order of 2 modulo n - 1), so following just index 1 until it returns produces the exact answer.
The answer must be positive — an initial check against zero steps is always wrong.

a.i: Apply the operation to the entire array repeatedly, comparing each result with the original identity. The number of operations is known to stay below n, so total work is O(n^2) in the worst case — entirely acceptable for n <= 1000 and the most direct reading of the problem.
s: Snapshot the initial array target = [0, 1, ..., n - 1].
Build the next array by the given parity rules from the current one.
Count each application and compare with target.
Return the count at the first exact match.
a.t: O(n * L) where L is the answer bounded by n - 2 — about 10^6 elementary steps at n = 1000.

a.n: Approach 2: Track a Single Index Through Its Cycle
a.i: Instead of whole arrays, follow only index 1. Under one operation its content relocates according to the same parity rule read as a position map: pos -> pos/2 when pos is even, pos -> n/2 + (pos - 1)/2 when pos is odd. Because the map is conjugate to doubling modulo n - 1, every other non-fixed index returns no later than index 1 does, so counting steps until pos hits 1 again yields the answer directly — O(cycle length) time and O(1) space.
s: Repeat: set pos to pos/2 if pos is even, else n/2 + (pos - 1)/2; increment steps.
Stop when pos equals 1 again and return steps.
a.t: O(L) — one step per operation until index 1 completes its cycle; L divides the multiplicative order of 2 modulo n - 1 and is under n.

w: In an interview, code the simulation first (it is hard to get wrong), then volunteer the single-index version as the optimization — being able to argue why index 1's cycle dominates (doubling mod n - 1) is what elevates the answer. Pitfalls: returning 0 because you compare before applying any operation, misreading which operand the parity rule indexes (it reads perm at a computed source position), and off-by-one errors in the odd branch formula. Edge cases: n = 2 (answer 1) and powers of two, where the answer is log2(n). Follow-up: state the closed form — the answer equals the multiplicative order of 2 modulo n - 1 — or generalize to arbitrary permutations by computing the lcm of all cycle lengths.
